clinicalPearls: A chronic sequela of deep vein thrombosis resulting from persistent venous obstruction and valvular damage that cause venous hypertension
Develops in a substantial proportion of patients after DVT, more commonly after proximal (iliofemoral) thrombosis and after recurrent ipsilateral DVT
Manifests as chronic limb pain, heaviness, swelling, cramps, itching, skin pigmentation and lipodermatosclerosis, and in severe cases venous ulceration
Symptoms are typically worse with standing and walking and relieved by rest and elevation; venous claudication may occur with iliac obstruction
Diagnosis is clinical and can be graded with the Villalta score, while venous duplex confirms reflux and residual obstruction
Risk is reduced by adequate initial anticoagulation, and in extensive iliofemoral DVT by early thrombus removal in selected patients
Management is largely conservative, with compression therapy, exercise, skin care, and leg elevation; iliac vein stenting may help selected patients with proximal obstruction
reference.pathophysiology: Post-thrombotic syndrome develops when a deep vein thrombus fails to resolve fully, leaving residual venous obstruction and destroying venous valves through inflammation and recanalisation. The combination of outflow obstruction and valvular reflux produces sustained ambulatory venous hypertension, transmitted to the microcirculation with the same downstream consequences as other chronic venous insufficiency, namely oedema, skin changes, and ulceration. Proximal (iliofemoral) thrombosis, recurrent thrombosis, and inadequate anticoagulation increase both the risk and the severity.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic venous insufficiency from primary valvular reflux
Iliac vein compression (May-Thurner) with residual obstruction
additionalInvestigations: Venous duplex ultrasound to assess reflux and residual obstruction
Clinical grading with the Villalta score
CT or MR venography for suspected iliac or caval obstruction amenable to stenting
Ankle-brachial pressure index before compression to exclude arterial disease
D-dimer and duplex to distinguish recurrent acute DVT from chronic changes
Ulcer assessment (swab, and biopsy if atypical) where ulceration is present
redFlags: Features suggesting recurrent acute DVT rather than chronic sequelae
A non-healing or atypical ulcer requiring biopsy
Coexisting significant arterial disease making compression hazardous
Rapidly progressive swelling suggesting new proximal obstruction or a mass
reference.prognosis: A chronic condition that can significantly impair quality of life; symptoms are often controllable with compression and lifestyle measures, but severe post-thrombotic syndrome with ulceration is difficult to treat, underscoring the importance of prevention.
pitfalls: Mistaking post-thrombotic changes for recurrent acute DVT, or the reverse
Under-using compression therapy, the mainstay of control
Applying compression without excluding arterial disease
references: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery and Endovascular Therapy
ESVS Clinical Practice Guidelines on Venous Disease
management: Graduated compression therapy with stockings or bandaging as the mainstay to counter ambulatory venous hypertension and control oedema
Adequate anticoagulation of the index deep vein thrombosis and prevention of recurrent ipsilateral thrombosis, the key to limiting severity
Exercise, leg elevation, weight management and meticulous skin care to reduce symptoms and protect vulnerable skin
Venous ulcer care with compression and appropriate dressings where ulceration has developed
Endovenous recanalisation and stenting for symptomatic iliac or caval obstruction, with early thrombus removal considered in extensive iliofemoral thrombosis
Analgesia and venoactive agents for chronic limb pain and heaviness, with referral to vascular services for refractory disease
